{{short description|Technique for visualizing complex functions}}
[[File:Complex-plot.png|270px|right|thumb|A [[domain coloring]] graph of the function
{{math|{{sfrac|(''z''<sup>2</sup> − 1)(''z'' − 2 − ''i'')<sup>2</sup>|''z''<sup>2</sup> + 2 + 2''i''}}}}. Darker spots mark moduli near zero, brighter spots are farther away from the origin. The color encodes the argument. The function has zeros for {{math|±1, (2 + ''i'')}} and [[pole (complex analysis)|poles]] at <math>\pm \sqrt{{-2-2i}}.</math>]]
In [[complex analysis]], '''domain coloring''' or a '''color wheel graph''' is a technique for [[scientific visualization#In mathematics|visualizing]] [[complex function]]s by assigning a [[color]] to each point of the [[complex plane]]. By assigning points on the complex plane to different colors and brightness, domain coloring allows for a function from the complex plane to itself, whose graph would normally require four spatial dimensions, to be easily represented and understood. This provides insight to the fluidity of complex functions and shows natural geometric extensions of [[real function]]s.

==Motivation==
A [[graph of a function|graph]] of a [[real function]] can be drawn in two dimensions because there are two represented variables, <math>x</math> and <math>y</math>. However, [[complex number]]s are represented by two variables and therefore two dimensions; this means that representing a complex function (more precisely, a [[complex-valued function]] of one [[complex variable]] <math>f: \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}</math>) requires the visualization of four dimensions. One way to achieve that is with a [[Riemann surface]], but another method is by domain coloring.

== History ==
The term "domain coloring" was coined by [[Frank Farris]], possibly around 1998.<ref>Frank A. Farris, [http://www.maa.org/pubs/amm_complements/complex.html Visualizing complex-valued functions in the plane]</ref><ref name="Ludmark1">{{Cite web |author=Hans Lundmark |year=2004 |title=Visualizing complex analytic functions using domain coloring |url=http://www.mai.liu.se/~halun/complex/domain_coloring-unicode.html |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20060502154939/http://www.mai.liu.se/~halun/complex/domain_coloring-unicode.html |archivedate=2006-05-02 |accessdate=2006-05-25}} Lundmark refers to Farris' coining the term "domain coloring" in this 2004 article.</ref> There were many earlier uses of color to visualize complex functions, typically mapping [[complex argument|argument]] ([[phase (waves)|phase]]) to hue.<ref>
{{cite journal |author=David A. Rabenhorst |date=1990 |title=A Color Gallery of Complex Functions |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DRUSAQAAMAAJ&q=%22phase%22+%22hue%22+complex-functions |journal=Pixel: The Magazine of Scientific Visualization |publisher=Pixel Communications |volume=1 |issue=4 |pages=42 et seq |issn=}}</ref>
[[Larry Crone]] used the method in the late 1980s.<ref>{{cite book |author=Elias Wegert |url=https://www.springer.com/us/book/9783034801799 |title=Visual Complex Functions: An Introduction with Phase Portraits |date=2012 |publisher=Springer Basel |isbn=9783034801799 |page=29 |accessdate=6 January 2016}}
</ref>
Dan Kucerovsky used it in 1990.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Kucerovsky |first=Dan |title=Conference Record of the 1990 IEEE Industry Applications Society Annual Meeting |date=October 1990 |isbn=0-87942-553-9 |pages=903–909 |chapter=An algorithm for the visual representation of a two-dimensional vector field |doi=10.1109/IAS.1990.152292 |chapter-url= |s2cid=34434375}}</ref> The technique of using continuous color to map points from domain to codomain or image plane was used in 1999 by George Abdo and Paul Godfrey<ref name="Abdo1">{{Cite web |author=George Abdo & Paul Godfrey |year=1999 |title=Plotting functions of a complex variable: Table of Conformal Mappings Using Continuous Coloring |url=http://my.fit.edu/~gabdo/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200316130844/http://my.fit.edu/~gabdo/ |archive-date=2020-03-16 |accessdate=2008-05-17}}</ref> and colored grids were used in graphics by [[Douglas N. Arnold|Doug Arnold]] that he dates to 1997.<ref name="Arnold1">{{Cite web |author=Douglas N. Arnold |authorlink=Douglas N. Arnold |year=2008 |title=Graphics for complex analysis |url=http://www.ima.umn.edu/~arnold/complex.html |accessdate=2008-05-17}}</ref>

== Method ==
{{multiple image
 | image1 = Identity domain coloring.svg
 | width1 = 200
 | image2 = Z^3 - 1 domain coloring.svg
 | width2 = 200
 | footer = HL plot of {{math|''z''}}, as per the simple color function example described in the text (left), and the graph of the complex function {{math|''z''<sup>3</sup>&nbsp;−&nbsp;1}} (right) using the same color function, showing the three zeros as well as the negative real numbers as pink rays starting at the zeros.
}}
Representing a four dimensional complex mapping with only two variables is undesirable, as methods like projections can result in a loss of information. However, it is possible to add variables that keep the four-dimensional process without requiring a visualization of four dimensions. In this case, the two added variables are visual inputs such as color and brightness because they are naturally two variables easily processed and distinguished by the human eye. This assignment is called a "color function". There are many different color functions used. A common practice is to represent the [[Argument (complex analysis)|complex argument]], <math>\arg z</math>, (also known as "phase" or "angle") with a [[hue]] following the [[color wheel]], and the [[magnitude (mathematics)|magnitude]] by other means, such as [[brightness]] or [[Colorfulness#Saturation|saturation]]. 

=== Simple color function ===
The following example colors the [[Origin (mathematics)|origin]] in black, {{math|1}} in [[green]], {{math|−1}} in [[magenta]], and a point at infinity in white:
<math display="block">\begin{cases}
H & = \arg z + 2\pi / 3,\\
S & = 100\%,\\
L & = \ell(|z|).
\end{cases}</math>
Where H is [[hue]], S is [[Colorfulness#Saturation|saturation]], and L is [[lightness]].
There are a number of choices for the function <math>\ell:[0, \infty)\to[0, 1)</math>.
<math>\ell</math> should be [[Monotonic function|strictly monotonic]] and [[Continuous function|continuous]].
Another desirable property is <math>\ell(1/r) = 1 - \ell(r)</math> such that
the inverse of a function is exactly as light as the original function is dark (and the other way around). Possible choices include 
* <math>\ell_1(r) = \frac{2}{\pi} \arctan(r)</math> and 
* <math>\ell_2(r) = \frac{r^a}{r^a+1}</math> (with some parameter <math>a>0</math>). With <math>a=2</math>, this corresponds to the [[stereographic projection]] onto the [[Riemann sphere]].

A widespread choice which does not have this property is the function <math>\ell_3(r) = 1 - a^{|r|}</math> (with some parameter <math>0 < a < 1</math>) which for <math>a=1/2</math> and <math>0\le r \le 1</math> is very close to <math>\ell_1</math>.

This approach uses the [[HSL color space|HSL]] (hue, saturation, lightness) color model. Saturation is always set at the maximum of 100%. Vivid colors of the rainbow are rotating in a continuous way on the complex unit circle, so the sixth [[Root of unity|roots of unity]] (starting with 1) are: green, cyan, blue, magenta, red, and yellow.

Since the HSL color space is not perceptually uniform, one can see streaks of perceived brightness at yellow, cyan, and magenta (even though their absolute values are the same as red, green, and blue) and a halo around {{math|1=''L'' = {{sfrac|1|2}}}}. More modern color spaces, e.g., the [[Lab color space]] or [[CIECAM02]], correct this, making the images more accurate and less saturated.
{{clear}}

===Discontinuous color changing===
Many color graphs have discontinuities, where instead of evenly changing brightness and color, it suddenly changes, even when the function itself is still smooth. This is done for a variety of reasons such as showing more detail or highlighting certain aspects of a function, like [[Level-set method|level sets]].

====Magnitude growth====
[[File:Domain coloring z 03.jpg|200px|right|thumb|A discontinuous color function. In the graph, each discontinuity occurs when <math>|z|=2^n</math> for integers ''n''.]]
Unlike the argument, which has finite range, the magnitude of a complex number can range from {{math|0}} to {{math|∞}}. Therefore, in functions that have large ranges of magnitude, changes in magnitude can sometimes be hard to differentiate when a very large change is also pictured in the graph. This can be remedied with a discontinuous color function which shows a repeating brightness pattern for the magnitude based on a given equation. This allows smaller changes to be easily seen as well as larger changes that "discontinuously jump" to a higher magnitude. In the graph on the right, these discontinuities occur in circles around the center, and show a dimming of the graph that can then start becoming brighter again. A similar color function has been used for the graph on top of the article.

Equations that determine the discontinuities may be linear, such as for every [[integer]] magnitude, exponential equations such as every magnitude <math>2^n</math> where ''n'' is an integer, or any other equation.

====Highlighting properties====
Discontinuities may be placed where outputs have a certain property to highlight which parts of the graph have that property. For instance, a graph may, instead of showing the color cyan, jump from green to blue. This causes a discontinuity that is easy to spot, and can highlight lines such as where the argument is zero.<ref>May 2004. http://users.mai.liu.se/hanlu09/complex/domain_coloring.html Retrieved 13 December 2018.</ref> Discontinuities may also affect large portions of a graph, such as a graph where the color wheel divides the graph into quadrants. In this way, it is easy to show where each quadrant ends up with relations to others.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Poelke |first1=K. |last2=Polthier |first2=K. |title=Domain Coloring of Complex Functions: An Implementation-Oriented Introduction |journal=IEEE Computer Graphics and Applications |date=September 2012 |volume=32 |issue=5 |pages=90–97 |doi=10.1109/MCG.2012.100 |pmid=24806991 |s2cid=19237225 }}</ref>

== Limitations ==
People who experience [[color blindness]] may have trouble interpreting such graphs when they are made with standard [[Color space|color maps]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=CET Perceptually Uniform Colour Maps|url=https://peterkovesi.com/projects/colourmaps/|access-date=2020-12-22|website=peterkovesi.com}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=Creating Symmetry: The Artful Mathematics of Wallpaper Patterns|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=blGUBgAAQBAJ&q=%22domain+coloring%22+color+blindness&pg=PA36|pages=36–37|first=Frank A.|last=Farris|date = 2 June 2015|isbn=978-0-691-16173-0|publisher=Princeton University Press}}</ref> This issue can be partially fixed by creating alternate versions using color maps that fit within the color space discernible to those with color blindness.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|last=Kovesi|first=Peter|date=2017|title=Colour Maps for the Colour Blind, presented at IAMG 2017|url=https://peterkovesi.com/papers/ColourMapsForColourBlindIAMG2017.pdf|access-date=|website=}}</ref> For example, for use by those with total [[Color blindness|deuteranopia]], a color map based on blue/grey/yellow may be more readable than the conventional map based on blue/green/red.<ref name=":0" />
